# Architecture decisions

Each decision states the choice, the reason and the consequence.

## 1. A static site with no framework

**Decision.** The site is plain HTML, one hand-written stylesheet and one small script. Pages are generated by Node.js scripts with no runtime dependencies.

**Why.** The content changes a few times a year, must be readable without JavaScript, and must work on GitHub Pages without a server. A framework would add a build pipeline and a runtime for no visible benefit.

**Consequence.** The only JavaScript is the theme toggle and the copy button. Both are progressive enhancements; the page is complete without them.

## 2. One content source, validated before rendering

**Decision.** All facts live in `content/*.json`. The build validates them (`scripts/lib/validate.mjs`) and refuses to continue on:

- skill percentages or proficiency numbers anywhere in `cv.json`;
- references to unknown projects, skill groups, concepts or diagrams;
- duplicate ids.

**Why.** The original site had proficiency bars (for example, Java 97%) that cannot be verified. Every page and every PDF must show the same facts, so the facts are written once.

**Consequence.** Adding a targeted CV means adding an entry to `variants.json`. Facts are never copied into a version.

## 3. Evidence labels instead of proficiency levels

**Decision.** Each skill carries `professional`, `personal` or `other`. The site shows the label as text and as a border style. The PDF lists `other` skills on a separate "Other skills" line.

**Why.** A skill is credible when it is linked to a role or project. A skill listed without that link must not look like proven experience. Apache Kafka is the current example: it appears in the source CV's skill list, but no role or project in the CV uses it.

**Consequence.** Moving a skill from `other` to `professional` is a deliberate content change. `tests/content.test.mjs` fails if Kafka is marked as professional before that decision is made.

## 4. The web resume and the PDF are the same page

**Decision.** Each targeted CV is one single-column HTML page. Chromium prints that page to A4 with the print stylesheet. There is no separate PDF template.

**Why.** One template means the PDF cannot drift from the web version. A single column with standard headings and plain text is what applicant-tracking systems parse best. Links stay clickable because Chromium keeps the `<a>` elements as PDF link annotations.

**Consequence.** The printed layout is controlled by `@media print` and `@page` in `assets/css/site.css`. The page count is checked by `tests/pdf.test.mjs`: targeted versions must fit two pages, the full CV three.

## 5. Generated output is committed

**Decision.** The generated HTML, SVG and PDF files are committed to the repository.

**Why.** GitHub Pages in legacy mode publishes the `main` branch as it is. Committing the output means the published site and the reviewed pull request are the same thing, and Pages needs no build step.

**Consequence.** Every content change must be built and committed together. CI rebuilds the site and fails if the committed HTML or SVG differs. PDFs are not compared byte for byte, because Chromium writes a creation timestamp; their content is checked by the PDF tests instead.

## 6. Browser testing with Playwright, PDF checks with poppler

**Decision.** Playwright runs the end-to-end tests and prints the PDFs. `pdfinfo` and `pdftotext` (poppler) check the PDFs.

**Why.** Playwright is already needed to print PDFs, so one browser engine covers both. Extracting text with poppler checks what an applicant-tracking system actually reads, which a JavaScript PDF library would not.

**Consequence.** The PDF tests need poppler installed. They are skipped with a notice where it is missing.

## 7. Diagrams are SVG with expandable components

**Decision.** Each architecture diagram is an SVG generated from `content/architecture.json`. The same data drives a list of components, where each component is a `<details>` element.

**Why.** Visitors can inspect a component without JavaScript, and the diagram and its explanation cannot disagree.

**Consequence.** The SVG labels must fit their boxes. `tests/content.test.mjs` limits each label to 46 characters.

## 8. Confidential detail is generalised

**Decision.** Diagram components and case studies use generic names and roles. Operational values from the earlier diagrams, such as state names and timer intervals, were removed.

**Why.** The task asked to avoid internal endpoints, infrastructure identifiers and proprietary implementation details. The remaining text describes behaviour, not configuration.

**Consequence.** `CONTENT_REVIEW.md` asks the owner to confirm that the generalised descriptions are acceptable.

## 9. Fonts and images are self-hosted

**Decision.** Inter (variable, latin subset, SIL Open Font License) is served from `assets/fonts/`. No third-party scripts, stylesheets or fonts are loaded.

**Why.** The site makes no requests outside its own domain except the links the reader follows. That keeps performance predictable and avoids tracking.

**Consequence.** The font file is about 47 KB. It is preloaded on every page.

## 10. What was removed and why

| Removed | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| jQuery 1.11, Bootstrap 3, Font Awesome 4 | Used only for layout and animated skill bars, which were removed. |
| Gulp, Sass, Less and the unused `theme-2` to `theme-6` folders | The stylesheet is now plain CSS. The Less themes were never referenced. |
| IE8/IE9 conditional comments and HTML5 shims | Not needed; the site targets current browsers. |
| Travis CI configuration | Built with Node 6 and an apt Yarn repository. Replaced by GitHub Actions. |
| `yarn.lock`, `.yarnclean` | npm is the only package manager now. |
| `build-tech-pages.js`, `build-project-diagrams.js`, `check-build.js` | Replaced by `scripts/` and the test suite. |
| Proficiency bars and the `level-bar` script | Replaced by evidence labels (decision 3). |
| Repository URLs `stden/stden.github.io` in `package.json` | Pointed at the wrong repository; now `stden/CV`. |
